title: Why Functions Exist
summary: Discover how to name a block of code so you can run it whenever you want.

content.title: The Repetition Problem, Again
content.summary: Copying the same lines over and over is a sign the code wants to become a function.
content.body:
You already know loops can repeat a single line. But what if you want to repeat a whole **group** of lines as one action?

Imagine a battle scene where the hero attacks:
content.codeBlock:
print("You raise your sword!")
print("Attack!")
print("The enemy takes damage.")
content.note: If you want that to happen three times, you're back to copy-pasting — or wrapping it all in a messy loop.

content.title: Inventing Your Own Command
content.summary: `def` lets you give a name to a block of code. After that, just write the name with `()` to run it.
content.body: Python lets you invent new commands. It's called **defining a function**:
content.codeBlock:
def attack():
    print("You raise your sword!")
    print("Attack!")
    print("The enemy takes damage.")
content.note:
Now `attack()` is a real command — just like `print()`. You call it by writing its name with parentheses:

```
attack()
attack()
attack()
```

content.title: Define Once, Use Many Times
content.summary: You define a function once at the top. Then call it as many times as you need.
content.body:
The `def` block runs zero times on its own — it just teaches Python what `attack()` means.

Every time you write `attack()`, Python runs the whole block from top to bottom.

Change the function once and every place that calls it automatically changes too. That is the power of functions.

content.title: The Two Steps
content.body: **Step 1 — Define** (teach Python what the function does):
content.note:
**Step 2 — Call** (actually run it) — that's the `jump()` line at the bottom.

If you skip step 1 and just write `jump()`, Python says: `NameError` — it has never heard of `jump`.
If you only do step 1 and never call it, nothing happens.

content.title: What is `pass`?
content.summary: `pass` is Python's "do nothing" placeholder — you'll see it in starter code.
content.body:
When you see a starter that looks like this:

```
def roar():
    pass
```

The word `pass` is Python's **"do nothing"** placeholder. Python needs at least one indented line inside every function, so `pass` is what we put there until you fill in the real code.

When you write your own lines, you can just delete the `pass`.

steps.instruction: Step 1: Replace `pass` inside `roar()` with one indented `print()` line — something like `print("ROAAAAR!")`. Run it. The roar should appear once (the call at the bottom is already there).
steps.starterCode:
# Step 1: define the function
def roar():
    pass  # replace this with your print lines

# Step 2: call it
roar()

steps.instruction: Step 2: Add a second indented `print()` line inside `roar()` (still 4 spaces in) describing more of the roar — maybe the ground shaking, or birds flying away. Run it. You should see two lines now.

Step 3: At the bottom, add a second `roar()` line below the first. Both calls should be at the **left margin** (no indent — they're outside the function). Run it — your roar block should print **twice**.

bonusSteps.instruction: Bonus: Define a second function called `cast_spell()` that prints a magic effect. Then build a battle sequence at the bottom: `roar()`, `cast_spell()`, `roar()`.

progressiveHints: Replace `pass` with two or three `print()` lines, each indented 4 spaces.
After the function definition (no indent), write `roar()` on a new line to call it.
To call it twice, add a second `roar()` line below the first.

Answer shape:
def roar():
    print("ROAAAAR!")
    print("The ground shakes.")

roar()
roar()
